fixture.description: Applied by the runner to a fresh database before each case. Adapters map these tables with their framework's own model or entity definitions.
fixture.sql: create table item (id serial primary key, name text not null, qty int not null default 0); create table uniq (id serial primary key, code text not null unique); insert into uniq (code) values ('taken');

CTL-01.title: Observation controls
CTL-01.question: Can the runner see, through its own connections, a transaction the framework committed, and the absence of one the framework rolled back? If not, the adapter's other results are not credible.

invariants.CTL-01.1: A transaction that the API reports as committed is committed: pg_xact_status() reports it committed, and an independent connection sees its marker.
invariants.CTL-01.2: A transaction that the API reports as rolled back is not committed: pg_xact_status() reports it aborted, and an independent connection does not see its marker.

TX-01A.title: Commit of an aborted transaction
TX-01A.question: A statement fails inside a transaction and the application catches the error. PostgreSQL has aborted the transaction, and answers the later COMMIT with ROLLBACK. Does the framework report a successful commit?

invariants.TX-01A.1: When PostgreSQL has aborted the transaction before it ends, so that its COMMIT is answered with ROLLBACK, the API does not report a successful commit.

TX-01B.title: Commit outcome after a connection or reply failure
TX-01B.question: The connection, or PostgreSQL's reply, is lost around COMMIT. Does the framework report only what it has evidence for?
TX-01B.notes: TX-01B.2 applies only where COMMIT may have reached PostgreSQL and no reply arrived. Where the client knows that COMMIT was never sent, a report of rollback is justified. TX-01B.2 is exercised only for adapters that observe a channel through which the framework could report a rollback; otherwise it is recorded as not exercised. A framework that verifies the outcome, for example with pg_xact_status() (which PostgreSQL documents for this purpose), and reports it, would still fail TX-01B.2: PPCS 0.1 does not evaluate such evidence.

invariants.TX-01B.1: When the connection or PostgreSQL's reply was lost around COMMIT, so that the client never received an acknowledgement of COMMIT, the API does not report a successful commit.
invariants.TX-01B.2: When COMMIT may have reached PostgreSQL and no reply arrived, the API does not report a confirmed rollback, through its result, its errors, or its rollback hooks or events.

TX-02.title: Failed savepoint rollback
TX-02.question: A nested scope fails, and its ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT fails too. Does the outer transaction silently continue under an incorrect nesting state: committing the failed scope's writes, reporting success for a transaction PostgreSQL did not commit, or leaving its transaction open after its API returned?

invariants.TX-02.1: If the API reports that the outer transaction committed, PostgreSQL committed it, with the outer scope's writes and none of the failed nested scope's writes.
invariants.TX-02.2: When the outer transaction's API has returned, the connection that ran it is no longer inside a transaction.

TX-03.title: Connection recovery and unsafe pool reuse
TX-03.question: A transaction fails on a pooled connection, and its ROLLBACK fails too. Does the pool give that connection to unrelated work while it still holds the failed transaction? Does the pool recover its capacity?

invariants.TX-03.1: Unrelated work never runs inside, or commits, a transaction whose rollback failed: that transaction is never committed, and the next unit of work runs in a transaction of its own.
invariants.TX-03.2: After the failure, the next unit of work on the same pool completes within the bound (settings.bound_ms) and commits.

TX-04.title: Nested transaction propagation
TX-04.question: When application code nests transactional work through an API that promises a propagation behaviour, does the work land in the transaction boundary the API promises?
TX-04.notes: Frameworks do not share propagation modes. Each case names the behaviour it tests. An adapter whose framework does not expose that behaviour through its supported API declares the case UNSUPPORTED in its manifest, which is not a failure, with a class: not-applicable-by-design where the hazard the case targets cannot arise by the framework's design (for example, no propagation modes and no deferred writes).

invariants.TX-04.1: When a nested scope (a savepoint) fails, and the caller handles the failure and commits, PostgreSQL commits all of the caller's writes and none of the nested scope's writes.
invariants.TX-04.2: A nested scope (a savepoint) that completed belongs to the outer transaction: when the outer transaction rolls back, the nested scope's writes are rolled back too.
invariants.TX-04.3: An inner transaction started through an API that promises an independent transaction commits only its own writes: the outer scope's writes, whether already sent or still pending in the framework, are committed only by the outer transaction.

TX-05.title: Requested isolation level
TX-05.question: When application code asks a framework's API to start a transaction at an isolation level that PostgreSQL supports, does the API either run the transaction at that level or refuse the request openly?
TX-05.notes: Every case requests SERIALIZABLE. A PASS needs two observations that agree. The first is PostgreSQL's own report, current_setting('transaction_isolation'), which the adapter reads in the same statement that captures the transaction's ID. The second comes from the runner's own connection: an SIReadLock held by that backend on item, or on an index of item, after a read of item that the runner confirmed by its AccessShareLock. The runner attributes each SIReadLock by its target, not by its count. It distinguishes SERIALIZABLE from weaker levels only. The binding to the transaction comes from PPCS's existing evidence: the captured ID is the backend's backend_xid, the backend holds the write's RowExclusiveLock and the read's AccessShareLock, and the visible marker's xmin is the captured ID. A rejected request counts against TX-05.2 only when its cause is established: no PostgreSQL SQLSTATE or operating-system error code, and a plain transaction through the same API form, started right after it, was bound at `baseline`. The ordering of levels is PostgreSQL's: READ UNCOMMITTED and READ COMMITTED, which PostgreSQL implements identically, then REPEATABLE READ, then SERIALIZABLE; another database engine would need its own, from its documented semantics. An adapter declares a case UNSUPPORTED (capability-absent) when its framework has no such API form, or documents that it does not support the requested level. Every INCONCLUSIVE result records a reason: observation-conflict, evidence-missing, environment, or cause-not-established.

invariants.TX-05.1: On PostgreSQL, a transaction that the API started at a requested isolation level runs at that level or a stricter one, never at a weaker one.
invariants.TX-05.2: An API whose documentation accepts an isolation level that PostgreSQL supports does not reject a valid request for that level: it starts the transaction.

cases.title: A transaction writes a marker and commits
steps: Start a transaction with the framework's ordinary transaction API.
Write the marker `tx` through the framework's ordinary write API.
Checkpoint `before-end`: report pg_current_xact_id() and pg_backend_pid(), read through the transaction's own connection.
End the transaction normally, so that the framework commits it.
Checkpoint `after-end`, as soon as the API has returned: the runner records the state at report time.
cases.knowledge: PostgreSQL answers COMMIT with the command tag COMMIT, so the client knows that the transaction committed.

cases.title: A transaction writes a marker and fails with an application error
steps: Start a transaction with the framework's ordinary transaction API.
Write the marker `tx`.
Checkpoint `before-end`: report pg_current_xact_id() and pg_backend_pid().
Raise an application error inside the transaction, so that the framework rolls it back.
Checkpoint `after-end`, as soon as the API has returned: the runner records the state at report time.
cases.knowledge: The framework rolls the transaction back, and PostgreSQL confirms the ROLLBACK, so the client knows that nothing committed.

cases.title: A unique violation is caught inside the transaction, which then ends normally
steps: Start a transaction with the framework's ordinary transaction API.
Write the marker `tx`, and make sure the write was sent to PostgreSQL.
Checkpoint `after-write`: report pg_current_xact_id() and pg_backend_pid(), read through the transaction's own connection.

Insert the value 'taken' into uniq through the framework's ordinary write API. It fails with unique_violation (23505). Catch the error and continue. After catching the error, the callback sends nothing else and returns.
Checkpoint `before-end`: report the same backend PID. The transaction is aborted, so it cannot run queries; the runner confirms the aborted state server-side.
End the transaction normally, so that the framework sends COMMIT.
Checkpoint `after-end`, as soon as the API has returned: the runner records the state at report time.

fault.mechanism: A unique_violation raised by PostgreSQL inside the transaction, and caught by the application.
fault.injection_point: After the first write, before the transaction ends.
fault.preconditions: The row 'taken' already exists in uniq (fixture).
fault.expected_server: The failed statement aborts the transaction. PostgreSQL answers the later COMMIT with the command tag ROLLBACK, without an error, and commits nothing.
fault.expected_client: The driver receives the command tag ROLLBACK as the reply to COMMIT.

cases.knowledge: The outcome reaches the client: PostgreSQL's reply to COMMIT carries the command tag ROLLBACK.

cases.title: The connection is terminated after the last write, before COMMIT
steps: Start a transaction with the framework's ordinary transaction API.
Write the marker `tx`.
Checkpoint `before-end`: report pg_current_xact_id() and pg_backend_pid(). The runner terminates that backend from its own connection, and waits until it has gone.
Wait settle_ms, so that the driver can observe the closed connection.
End the transaction normally, so that the framework attempts to commit.
Checkpoint `after-end`, as soon as the API has returned: the runner records the state at report time.

fault.mechanism: pg_terminate_backend(pid), run by the runner from its own connection.
fault.injection_point: After the last write, before the framework sends COMMIT.
fault.preconditions: The PID the adapter reports belongs to the case's database.
fault.expected_server: The backend exits, and its transaction is rolled back.
fault.expected_client: A connection error at COMMIT. No reply to COMMIT can arrive.

cases.knowledge: Known not committed: the session ended before the framework tried to commit, so the driver refused to send COMMIT ("Client has encountered a connection error and is not queryable"). A report of rollback is justified; a report of success is not.

cases.title: COMMIT completes on the server, and the client discards the reply (client-side simulation)
steps: Start a transaction with the framework's ordinary transaction API.
Write the marker `tx`.
Checkpoint `before-end`: report pg_current_xact_id() and pg_backend_pid().
Arm the client-side fault: the driver sends the next COMMIT, which PostgreSQL executes; the driver then closes its own connection and reports a connection error instead of the reply.
End the transaction normally, so that the framework sends COMMIT.
Checkpoint `after-end`, as soon as the API has returned: the runner records the state at report time.

fault.mechanism: A client-side simulation inside the adapter's driver layer (node-postgres, pg.Client.prototype.query): COMMIT is sent and completes on the server; the client then closes its own connection, and the caller receives a connection error instead of the reply. It is not a network failure. Artifact: the driver has already parsed PostgreSQL's reply (its transaction status reads idle) before the simulated loss, where a real loss leaves it reading in-transaction. The case therefore establishes only whether the API claims an outcome after its COMMIT call fails, not behaviour that depends on the driver's state, such as pool recovery.
fault.injection_point: In the client, between the server's reply to COMMIT and its delivery to the framework.
fault.preconditions: The framework's statements pass through the instrumented pg module (recorded as trace_sees_framework_pg).
fault.expected_client: A connection error in place of the reply to COMMIT.

cases.knowledge: None at the API level: the reply to COMMIT was discarded before the framework saw it. Only a later read can establish that the transaction committed.

cases.title: COMMIT completes on the server, and the network drops the reply before the client reads it
steps: Start a transaction with the framework's ordinary transaction API. The runner places a protocol proxy between the client and PostgreSQL.
Write the marker `tx`.
Checkpoint `before-end`: report pg_current_xact_id() and pg_backend_pid().

End the transaction normally, so that the framework sends COMMIT. The proxy forwards COMMIT, reads PostgreSQL's reply through ReadyForQuery, does not write that reply to the client, and closes the client socket.
Checkpoint `after-end`, as soon as the API has returned: the runner records the state at report time.

fault.mechanism: The runner's protocol proxy forwards COMMIT to PostgreSQL, then discards the reply through ReadyForQuery and closes the client socket. The client does not parse the reply. This is not the category D simulation, which closes the socket after node-postgres has already parsed the reply.
fault.injection_point: On the wire, after PostgreSQL has written the COMMIT reply and before the client reads it.
fault.expected_client: The connection closes where the reply to COMMIT would have been read.

cases.knowledge: None at the API level: the reply to COMMIT was not delivered. Only a later read can establish that the transaction committed.

cases.title: A nested scope fails, and its ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT fails on the client
steps: Start the outer transaction with the framework's ordinary transaction API, on a pool of one connection.
Write the marker `outer`, and make sure the write was sent.
Checkpoint `outer-after-write`: report pg_current_xact_id() and pg_backend_pid().
Start a nested scope with the framework's nested-transaction (savepoint) API. Write the marker `inner` in it, and make sure the write was sent.
Checkpoint `inner-after-write`: report the backend PID. The runner sees the savepoint's subtransaction lock.
Arm the client-side fault (the next ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT fails in the driver and is not sent), then raise an application error in the nested scope.
When the fault fires, before the framework sees its error, the adapter's driver layer reports checkpoint `after-fault` (the backend PID): the runner records the fault's effect on the server.
The outer scope catches the nested scope's error.
The outer scope ends normally.
Checkpoint `after-outer`, after the outer transaction's API has returned: report the same backend PID. The runner records whether that session is still inside a transaction.
Checkpoint `after-end`, as soon as the API has returned: the runner records the state at report time.

fault.mechanism: A client-side injection in the adapter's driver layer (node-postgres, pg.Client.prototype.query): ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT fails without being sent, as a failed send would.
fault.injection_point: The framework's rollback of the nested scope.
fault.preconditions: The framework's statements pass through the instrumented pg module (recorded as trace_sees_framework_pg).
fault.expected_server: The savepoint is never rolled back: the nested scope's write stays in the outer transaction.
fault.expected_client: An error from the nested scope's rollback; what the framework then does is under test.

cases.knowledge: The framework knows that its savepoint rollback failed, so it knows that the nested scope's writes may still be in the transaction.

cases.title: A nested scope fails, and PostgreSQL rejects its ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT
steps: Start the outer transaction with the framework's ordinary transaction API, on a pool of one connection.
Write the marker `outer`, and make sure the write was sent.
Checkpoint `outer-after-write`: report pg_current_xact_id() and pg_backend_pid().
Start a nested scope with the framework's nested-transaction (savepoint) API. Write the marker `inner` in it, and make sure the write was sent.
Checkpoint `inner-after-write`: report the backend PID. The runner sees the savepoint's subtransaction lock.
Arm the client-side fault (the next ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT is rewritten to name a savepoint that does not exist, so PostgreSQL rejects it), then raise an application error in the nested scope.
When the fault fires, before the framework sees its error, the adapter's driver layer reports checkpoint `after-fault` (the backend PID): the runner records the fault's effect on the server.
The outer scope catches the nested scope's error.
The outer scope ends normally.
Checkpoint `after-outer`, after the outer transaction's API has returned: report the same backend PID. The runner records whether that session is still inside a transaction.
Checkpoint `after-end`, as soon as the API has returned: the runner records the state at report time.

fault.mechanism: A client-side injection in the adapter's driver layer: ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT is rewritten before it is sent, to name a savepoint that does not exist. PostgreSQL rejects it with 3B001, which aborts the current subtransaction (the savepoint's). The error is PostgreSQL's; the trigger is artificial.
fault.injection_point: The framework's rollback of the nested scope.
fault.preconditions: The framework's statements pass through the instrumented pg module (recorded as trace_sees_framework_pg).
fault.expected_server: The savepoint's subtransaction is aborted: the session is "idle in transaction (aborted)" while the top-level transaction stays in progress. A ROLLBACK TO the existing savepoint recovers it; a COMMIT without recovery is answered with ROLLBACK, and commits nothing.
fault.expected_client: A PostgreSQL error from the nested scope's rollback.

cases.knowledge: The framework receives PostgreSQL's error (3B001) for the savepoint rollback. If it then sends COMMIT without recovering, it receives the command tag ROLLBACK.

cases.title: The connection is terminated inside a nested scope that then fails
steps: Start the outer transaction with the framework's ordinary transaction API, on a pool of one connection.
Write the marker `outer`, and make sure the write was sent.
Checkpoint `outer-after-write`: report pg_current_xact_id() and pg_backend_pid().
Start a nested scope with the framework's nested-transaction (savepoint) API. Write the marker `inner` in it, and make sure the write was sent.
Checkpoint `inner-after-write`: report the backend PID. The runner sees the savepoint's subtransaction lock. The runner then terminates the backend, and waits until it has gone.
Wait settle_ms, then raise an application error in the nested scope; its ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT fails on the closed connection.
The outer scope catches the nested scope's error.
The outer scope ends normally.
Checkpoint `after-outer`, after the outer transaction's API has returned: report the same backend PID. The runner records whether that session is still inside a transaction.
Checkpoint `after-end`, as soon as the API has returned: the runner records the state at report time.

fault.mechanism: pg_terminate_backend(pid), run by the runner from its own connection.
fault.injection_point: Inside the nested scope, after its write, before the framework's savepoint rollback.
fault.preconditions: The PID the adapter reports belongs to the case's database.
fault.expected_server: The backend exits, and the whole transaction is rolled back.
fault.expected_client: Connection errors for the savepoint rollback and for anything after it.

cases.knowledge: The framework sees its connection fail during the savepoint rollback.

cases.title: The top-level ROLLBACK of a failed transaction fails on the client; then the next unit of work runs on the same pool
steps: Unit 1: start a transaction with the framework's ordinary transaction API, on a pool of one connection.
Write the marker `doomed`.
Checkpoint `unit1-after-write`: report pg_current_xact_id() and pg_backend_pid(). Then arm the client-side fault: the next top-level ROLLBACK fails in the driver and is not sent.
Raise an application error inside the transaction. The framework attempts ROLLBACK, which fails, so the connection keeps its open transaction.
When the fault fires, before the framework sees its error, the adapter's driver layer reports checkpoint `after-fault` (the backend PID): the runner records the fault's effect on the server.
Checkpoint `after-unit1`: report the same backend PID; the runner records that session's state.

Unit 2, the next unit of work on the same pool: start a transaction, write the marker `next`, checkpoint `unit2-after-write` (report pg_current_xact_id() and pg_backend_pid()), and end normally. Give up after settings.bound_ms and report the unit as pending.
Checkpoint `after-end`, as soon as the API has returned: the runner records the state at report time.

fault.mechanism: A client-side injection in the adapter's driver layer (node-postgres, pg.Client.prototype.query): the top-level ROLLBACK fails without being sent, as a failed send would.
fault.preconditions: The framework's statements pass through the instrumented pg module (recorded as trace_sees_framework_pg).
fault.expected_server: Unit 1's transaction stays open on its connection ("idle in transaction"), holding the doomed write.
fault.expected_client: An error from the framework's rollback; what the framework then does with the connection is under test.

cases.knowledge: The framework knows that its ROLLBACK failed, so it knows that the connection's transaction state is unknown.

cases.title: A statement fails inside a transaction and its top-level ROLLBACK fails on the client; then the next unit of work runs on the same pool
steps: Unit 1: start a transaction with the framework's ordinary transaction API, on a pool of one connection.
Write the marker `doomed`.
Checkpoint `unit1-after-write`: report pg_current_xact_id() and pg_backend_pid(). Then arm the client-side fault: the next top-level ROLLBACK fails in the driver and is not sent.

Insert the value 'taken' into uniq through the framework's ordinary write API, and do not catch the error. It fails with unique_violation (23505), which aborts the transaction. The framework attempts ROLLBACK, which fails, so the connection stays in its aborted transaction block.
When the fault fires, before the framework sees its error, the adapter's driver layer reports checkpoint `after-fault` (the backend PID): the runner records the fault's effect on the server.
Checkpoint `after-unit1`: report the same backend PID; the runner records that session's state.

Unit 2, the next unit of work on the same pool: start a transaction, write the marker `next`, checkpoint `unit2-after-write` (report pg_current_xact_id() and pg_backend_pid()), and end normally. Give up after settings.bound_ms and report the unit as pending.
Checkpoint `after-end`, as soon as the API has returned: the runner records the state at report time.

fault.mechanism: A unique_violation raised by PostgreSQL inside unit 1, which aborts its transaction, then a client-side injection in the adapter's driver layer (node-postgres, pg.Client.prototype.query): the top-level ROLLBACK fails without being sent, as a failed send would.
fault.injection_point: The framework's ROLLBACK of unit 1, after the failed statement.
fault.preconditions: The row 'taken' already exists in uniq (fixture). The framework's statements pass through the instrumented pg module (recorded as trace_sees_framework_pg).
fault.expected_server: Unit 1's transaction is already aborted: pg_xact_status() reports it aborted, and it holds no locks. Its connection stays in the aborted transaction block ("idle in transaction (aborted)"), where every statement except ROLLBACK fails with 25P02.
fault.expected_client: The unique violation, then an error from the framework's rollback; what the framework then does with the connection is under test. A unit of work given the connection as it is fails loudly with 25P02, instead of silently joining the open transaction as in TX-03.rollback-not-sent.

cases.knowledge: The framework received PostgreSQL's error for the failed statement, and knows that its ROLLBACK failed, so it knows that the connection is still inside a transaction block.

cases.title: The backend of a failing transaction is terminated before its ROLLBACK; then the next unit of work runs on the same pool
steps: Unit 1: start a transaction with the framework's ordinary transaction API, on a pool of one connection.

Checkpoint `unit1-after-write`: report pg_current_xact_id() and pg_backend_pid(). The runner terminates that backend and waits until it has gone. Then wait settle_ms.
Raise an application error inside the transaction. The framework attempts ROLLBACK on the closed connection, which fails.
Checkpoint `after-unit1`: report the same backend PID; the runner records that session's state.

Unit 2, the next unit of work on the same pool: start a transaction, write the marker `next`, checkpoint `unit2-after-write` (report pg_current_xact_id() and pg_backend_pid()), and end normally. Give up after settings.bound_ms and report the unit as pending.
Checkpoint `after-end`, as soon as the API has returned: the runner records the state at report time.

fault.mechanism: pg_terminate_backend(pid), run by the runner from its own connection.
fault.injection_point: Inside unit 1, after its write, before the framework's ROLLBACK.
fault.preconditions: The PID the adapter reports belongs to the case's database.
fault.expected_server: The backend exits, and unit 1's transaction is rolled back.
fault.expected_client: An error from the framework's rollback; the pool holds a closed connection.

cases.knowledge: The framework knows that its connection failed.

cases.title: A nested scope fails; the caller handles the failure and commits
steps: Start the outer transaction with the framework's ordinary transaction API.
Write the marker `outer` through the framework's ordinary write API. The framework decides when it is sent: one with a unit of work may keep it pending.
Start a nested scope with the framework's nested-transaction (savepoint) API. Write the marker `inner` in it, and make sure that write was sent.
Checkpoint `inner-after-write`: report pg_current_xact_id() (the top-level transaction's ID) and pg_backend_pid().
Raise an application error in the nested scope.
The outer scope catches the error and ends normally.
Checkpoint `after-end`, as soon as the API has returned: the runner records the state at report time.
cases.knowledge: The caller knows that the nested scope failed: its error reached the caller. PostgreSQL answers the final COMMIT with COMMIT.

cases.title: A nested scope completes; then the outer transaction rolls back
steps: Start the outer transaction with the framework's ordinary transaction API.
Write the marker `outer` through the framework's ordinary write API. The framework decides when it is sent: one with a unit of work may keep it pending.
Start a nested scope with the framework's nested-transaction (savepoint) API. Write the marker `inner` in it, and make sure that write was sent.
Checkpoint `inner-after-write`: report pg_current_xact_id() and pg_backend_pid().
End the nested scope normally, so that its savepoint is released.
Raise an application error in the outer scope, so that the framework rolls the outer transaction back.
Checkpoint `after-end`, as soon as the API has returned: the runner records the state at report time.
cases.knowledge: The caller knows that the nested scope completed, and that the outer transaction rolled back.

cases.title: An inner transaction that promises independence commits; then the outer transaction rolls back
steps: Start the outer transaction with the framework's ordinary transaction API, on a pool of two connections.
Write the marker `outer` through the framework's ordinary write API. The framework decides when it is sent: one with a unit of work may keep it pending.
Start an inner transaction through the framework's API that promises an independent transaction (for example a REQUIRES_NEW propagation). Write the marker `inner` in it.
Checkpoint `inner-after-write`: report the inner transaction's pg_current_xact_id() and pg_backend_pid().
End the inner transaction normally, so that it commits.
Raise an application error in the outer scope, so that the framework rolls the outer transaction back.
Checkpoint `after-end`, as soon as the API has returned: the runner records the state at report time.
cases.knowledge: The caller knows that the inner transaction committed and the outer one rolled back. From the API alone, it cannot see which transaction carried a write the framework still had pending.

cases.title: A managed transaction requests SERIALIZABLE
steps: Start a transaction with the framework's managed transaction API, the one that runs a callback inside the transaction and commits when it returns, requesting the isolation level in settings.isolation_level (SERIALIZABLE). The server's default is READ COMMITTED. If the API raises instead of starting the transaction, record its error and go to step 6.
Write the marker `tx` through the framework's ordinary write API, and make sure that write was sent.

Read the marker back through the framework's ordinary query API, inside the same transaction, and make sure the read reached PostgreSQL: a query, not a lookup in the framework's identity map or cache. The runner confirms it by the transaction's AccessShareLock on item.
Checkpoint `after-read`: in one statement, through the transaction's own connection, read pg_current_xact_id(), pg_backend_pid() and current_setting('transaction_isolation'), and report all three.
Return from the callback normally, so that the framework commits the transaction. Then go to the last step.

Only if the API raised at step 1: start a plain transaction through the same managed API, with no isolation level. Inside it, at checkpoint `baseline`, report pg_current_xact_id() and pg_backend_pid(), then end it normally. If the plain transaction fails too, report its error in steps.baseline. Report the outcome failed, with step 1's error as api_error.
Checkpoint `after-end`, as soon as the API has returned (after step 6, when it ran): the runner records the state at report time.
cases.knowledge: A successful start does not tell the application which level PostgreSQL applied; only current_setting('transaction_isolation'), read inside the transaction, does. An application that requested SERIALIZABLE and got no error relies on its guarantee: concurrent transactions behave as if they had run one at a time. A rejected request reaches the application as an error, so it can decide what to do instead.

cases.title: An explicit transaction requests SERIALIZABLE
steps: Start a transaction with the framework's explicit transaction API, the one that returns a transaction handle which the application commits with an explicit call, requesting the isolation level in settings.isolation_level (SERIALIZABLE). The server's default is READ COMMITTED. If the API raises instead of starting the transaction, record its error and go to step 6.
Write the marker `tx` through the framework's ordinary write API, using the handle, and make sure that write was sent.

Read the marker back through the framework's ordinary query API, using the handle, and make sure the read reached PostgreSQL: a query, not a lookup in the framework's identity map or cache. The runner confirms it by the transaction's AccessShareLock on item.
Checkpoint `after-read`: in one statement, through the transaction's own connection, read pg_current_xact_id(), pg_backend_pid() and current_setting('transaction_isolation'), and report all three.
Commit with the handle's explicit commit call. Then go to the last step.

Only if the API raised at step 1: start a plain transaction through the same explicit API, with no isolation level. Inside it, at checkpoint `baseline`, report pg_current_xact_id() and pg_backend_pid(), then end it normally. If the plain transaction fails too, report its error in steps.baseline. Report the outcome failed, with step 1's error as api_error.
Checkpoint `after-end`, as soon as the API has returned (after step 6, when it ran): the runner records the state at report time.
cases.knowledge: A successful start does not tell the application which level PostgreSQL applied; only current_setting('transaction_isolation'), read inside the transaction, does. An application that requested SERIALIZABLE and got no error relies on its guarantee: concurrent transactions behave as if they had run one at a time. A rejected request reaches the application as an error, so it can decide what to do instead.
